item.title: Congressional Democrats Target Equipment Expensing Rules for Data Centers
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Democratic lawmakers propose ending bonus depreciation for data center equipment, raising $30 billion as political opposition to the sector intensifies nationwide.

The post Congressional Democrats Target Equipment Expensing Rules for Data Centers appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic lawmakers have introduced multiple bills to eliminate bonus depreciation for data center equipment, a tax provision that allows developers to immediately expense server racks, GPUs, and other capital costs rather than deduct them over the equipment’s lifetime. Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia introduced the Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act in July, which would raise nearly $30 billion over 10 years by barring full expensing for data center owners. Senate Finance Ranking Member Ron Wyden of Oregon proposed going further, blocking data centers from Opportunity Zone incentives and REIT benefits in addition to bonus depreciation. Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, who won election to the Senate this week, has also introduced legislation targeting the same tax treatment.

Democrats gained control of Congress in the recent midterm elections, though any legislation must still pass President Trump. Tax policy experts at the Tax Foundation and BDO note that while full expensing under Section 168(k) has enjoyed bipartisan support for manufacturers and other industries, the proposals targeting data centers reflect a broader political backlash against the sector. Andrew Lautz of the Tax Foundation said the energy behind these bills is directed specifically at data centers, not at equipment expensing more broadly. The proposals may set the agenda for future tax legislation if Democrats regain the presidency.

Opposition to data centers has grown sharply over the past year, with 47 local ballot measures limiting AI data center development passing in the midterm elections. Permit approval rates for data centers fell to 34% in the third quarter from 54% in 2025, according to Spark. Polling from Heatmap shows 75% of Americans now oppose data centers near their homes, up from 42% in August 2025. Developers face more restrictive zoning, permitting requirements, and demands for community benefits even as over $1 trillion in capital flows into data center construction nationwide.

The Business Journals
A Data-Center-Friendly Tax Credit May Become a Target in 2027

item.title: A Blue Wave Meets a Veto Pen: What the Midterms Mean for CRE
item.dc:creator: Travis Barrington
item.description:
Democrats swept Congress, but Trump’s veto means the energy and tax changes affecting commercial real estate are likely to stand through 2028.

The post A Blue Wave Meets a Veto Pen: What the Midterms Mean for CRE appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January after an election night that went worse for Republicans than almost anyone in either party predicted. As of Wednesday morning they had secured at least 228 House seats and 54 Senate seats, with dozens of House races still being counted and network projections running considerably higher. The Senate map was the biggest surprise, with Democrats flipping seats in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina, several of which were not considered competitive a year ago. About two-thirds of voters told an election-day survey that tariffs had hurt the economy, and gas prices tied to the war with Iran weighed on Republican candidates almost everywhere.

Markets mostly shrugged. Stock futures dipped overnight before recovering, the 10-year Treasury yield fell a few basis points to between 4.90% and 4.94%, and oil and the dollar both slipped modestly, according to Cushman & Wakefield. Investors seem to understand that winning Congress and governing from it are very different things while Donald Trump still holds the veto.

Trump made that point himself on election night, posting an image of a red cap with “VETO” stitched across the front. On Wednesday he told reporters that Democrats would “send over things that are insane and I’ll veto them,” though he also said he expected to work with the new majority on some issues. Overriding a veto requires two-thirds of both chambers, which means 290 votes in the House and 67 in the Senate, and Democrats are nowhere near either number. Most legislation also has to clear a Senate filibuster that requires 60 votes. Budget reconciliation gets around the filibuster with a simple majority, but a reconciliation bill still ends up on the president’s desk.

Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become Speaker, has promised to restore Medicaid funding and Affordable Care Act subsidies, roll back tariffs and end the war with Iran. Each of those goals depends on Trump signing something he opposes or on enough Republicans breaking with him to override his veto. Some defections are plausible, since Trump is in his final two years and Republicans who just watched colleagues lose in Kansas and Texas have reason to keep some distance from the White House, particularly on tariffs. Getting to two-thirds is another matter, and party discipline usually erodes one narrow vote at a time.

For commercial real estate, the federal policies with the most direct effect on buildings are already written into law. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed in July 2025, cut short much of the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean energy package. Owners felt it most through Section 179D, the energy-efficient commercial buildings deduction, which does not apply to projects that began construction after June 30, 2026. The 45L credit for efficient new homes and the 30C credit for EV charging equipment ran into similar deadlines. Bringing any of them back would take a new tax bill with Trump’s signature on it, which is unlikely before he leaves office. The same law made 100% bonus depreciation permanent, a provision the industry lobbied hard for, and Democrats can’t repeal it over his objection any more than they can restore 179D. Owners can reasonably assume the tax code they are working with today is the one they will have in 2028.

Tariffs rest on executive power rather than legislation. After the Supreme Court struck down the emergency tariffs in February, the administration reissued them under other trade authorities that Congress had delegated years ago. A Democratic Congress can hold hearings and apply pressure, but it cannot change that policy on its own, so the cost of steel, aluminum and other building materials will keep following decisions made at the White House.

Where Democrats do gain real power is in their ability to slow things down. Control of both chambers gives them appropriations, committee chairmanships and subpoena authority, and Cushman & Wakefield expects divided government to raise the odds of a debt-limit fight, government shutdowns and more unilateral trade action from the executive branch. The White House has reportedly spent months preparing to advance its agenda without going through Congress at all. Policy made by executive order can change quickly and be reversed just as quickly, and that kind of uncertainty is harder for lenders and investors to price than a statute that will sit on the books for years.

The larger variable for property values is the war. Vice President JD Vance blamed Tuesday’s losses on the Iran conflict, and Trump pointed to gas prices. Cushman & Wakefield considers the war the primary swing factor for inflation and interest rates, and in a market priced off the 10-year Treasury, that matters more than which party runs the House.

Past midterms offer little reason to expect a shift in property markets. Since 1978, private real estate returns in the year following a midterm have looked about the same as returns in any other year, according to Cushman & Wakefield, and REITs, which reprice faster, show the same pattern. The firm did not change its economic outlook after Tuesday, because a divided Congress was already part of its baseline. It expects growth slightly above 2%, inflation that stays elevated before gradually easing, and a 10-year yield between 4.5% and 5.0% through 2027.

That outlook is reasonably good for occupiers. Continued growth should support demand for space across most property types, and with little new construction in the pipeline, rents should rise, especially in the highest-quality buildings. For investors, Cushman & Wakefield expects returns to come from rising income rather than falling cap rates, so interest rates, economic growth and the performance of individual properties will matter far more over the next two years than anything that happens on Capitol Hill.

The post A Blue Wave Meets a Veto Pen: What the Midterms Mean for CRE appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Cross-Border Property Losses Trigger Criminal Probe at German Pension Fund
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Munich prosecutors raided an asset manager over US property investments that may cost Germany's largest public pension fund €853 million.

The post Cross-Border Property Losses Trigger Criminal Probe at German Pension Fund appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Munich prosecutors raided Deutsche Finance on Tuesday as part of an investigation into US real estate investments that produced substantial losses for BVK, Germany’s largest public-sector pension fund. BVK oversees €122 billion in retirement assets for 2.8 million Bavarians and has flagged potential write-offs of as much as €853 million on US properties linked to Deutsche Finance and New York developer Michael Shvo’s firm SHVO. Deutsche Finance confirmed the search and said it is cooperating as a third party, while prosecutors declined to specify the focus of their probe. Süddeutsche Zeitung reported the investigation centers on allegations of bribery through trips and amenities.

BVK invested roughly €1.6 billion in a portfolio of US trophy assets including the Transamerica Pyramid in San Francisco, 685 Fifth Avenue and 711 Fifth Avenue in New York, 9200 Wilshire Boulevard in Los Angeles, and 333 South Wabash in Chicago. By the end of last year, the pension group had already written off €392 million of those investments. SHVO said earlier this year that the properties are outperforming the market with record rents and blue-chip tenants, while Deutsche Finance said in January that its US subsidiary had no discretionary authority over investment selection or execution.

Two senior BVK managers departed after an internal investigation found compliance violations, including lavish business trips. German prosecutors have not accused Shvo or his firm of wrongdoing, and neither Deutsche Finance nor the prosecutors mentioned SHVO in their Tuesday communications. Germany’s vocational pension fund industry, which manages roughly €300 billion in retirement savings, operates under fragmented supervision and is often overseen by people with limited investing experience.

Several German vocational pension funds have surfaced as backers of US real estate developments and other investments that faltered when interest rates rose. BVK’s losses have intensified scrutiny of governance practices across the €300 billion sector, which forms a critical piece of Germany’s retirement infrastructure. The Munich prosecutors’ office said it will release additional details on the investigation in the coming days.

German Raid Adds to Scrutiny of Pension Fund’s US Property Deals

item.title: Four Brokerages Form Shared Listing System to Counter Compass Strategy
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
AGNT, HomeServices, Keller Williams and REMAX back Open Real Estate, a shared listing platform challenging Compass's private-listing strategy amid federal lawsuits.

The post Four Brokerages Form Shared Listing System to Counter Compass Strategy appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
AGNT, HomeServices of America, Keller Williams and Real REMAX Group announced Oct. 26 they are backing Open Real Estate, a shared listing platform designed to distribute property data across multiple listing services and authorized websites. Participating brokerages would be required to submit new listings within one business day of signing a seller agreement. Brown Harris Stevens, Lamacchia Realty, Samson Properties and Windermere are among the initial participants, with the four founding companies covering the cost of building the technology at no initial charge to members.

Six regional multiple listing services representing more than 120,000 real estate professionals filed a federal lawsuit against Compass last month seeking to enforce rules requiring brokers to share property listings. OneKey MLS in New York has since joined a separate lawsuit brought by California Regional Multiple Listing Service. Compass has expanded its private-listing network, arguing that homeowners should control when and how their properties are advertised; the company’s research shows sellers who first marketed properties as Private Exclusives or Coming Soons achieved sale prices 4.6% higher than comparable homes listed directly on the MLS and went under contract 34% faster.

Open Real Estate includes a “participant view” feature allowing certain properties to be shared exclusively among agents at participating brokerages without public marketing, similar to a system used by the Real Estate Board of New York. Brown Harris Stevens CEO Bess Freedman said the feature would accommodate a small percentage of sellers requesting privacy for security or personal reasons, while the broader platform aims to prevent data hoarding. Compass CEO Robert Reffkin said the new national listing service would return greater control to homeowners and their agents, and Open Real Estate’s founders said Compass would be welcome to join the platform.

The initiative comes after Compass completed a $1.6 billion merger with Anywhere Real Estate, bringing major brokerage brands under the same corporate umbrella. Open Real Estate would operate alongside existing multiple listing services rather than replace them. A Compass spokesperson said the company is challenging industry rules so homeowners can market their homes publicly even if they choose channels other than the MLS or Zillow, arguing that the law does not require homeowners to give those private companies their data.

New York Post
Real Estate Giants Launch National Home Database as Battle Over ‘Private’ Listings Heats Up

item.title: How AI Is Compressing Real Estate Decision Timelines
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
AI is reshaping commercial real estate, accelerating deal screening, underwriting, lending, and portfolio decisions as planning horizons shrink.

The post How AI Is Compressing Real Estate Decision Timelines appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Real estate has always been a slow business by design. Leases run seven to ten years. Diligence takes weeks. Underwriting assumes conditions that hold across a hold period measured in cycles rather than quarters. The pace has been a feature, giving investors time to be deliberate about commitments that are expensive to reverse.

That timeline no longer matches how the businesses occupying the space operate. JLL’s Future of Work research, which surveyed 2,200 C-suite executives and CRE leaders across 21 countries, found innovation-intensive sectors have compressed their planning horizons to somewhere between 12 and 24 months. Most lease renewals are still being evaluated against assumptions that run seven to ten years out, which means the income underwriting a deal rests on a forecast the tenant may no longer be making.

Ram Srinivasan, Managing Director of AI Adoption, AI Integration and Future of Work Advisory at JLL, describes the mismatch as a problem with the decision model rather than with the leases themselves. “Real estate decisions are long-term commitments, but businesses no longer have the luxury of thinking seven years in advance,” he said. “The decision-making model needs to evolve.”

AI is compressing the analysis side at the same time it compresses the planning side. Daniel Rooney, Managing Director at JLL Consulting, ran the same engagement both ways to see what the difference looked like. “We ran a client’s full portfolio analytics two ways,” he said. “The traditional manual process took four weeks. The AI-assisted version took minutes.”

For an asset manager evaluating acquisitions, that collapse changes which deals are even worth looking at. A multi-week analysis cycle forces triage. Opportunities get screened on surface characteristics because fully underwriting them is too expensive to do speculatively, and the ones that survive get modeled against a narrow set of scenarios. Three hours spent on a deal that fails screening is three hours an analyst could have spent on one that did not.

Deal screening has emerged as its own product category in response. Both Dealpath and Altrio launched dedicated screening tools in 2026, treating the job of scoring an inbound offering memorandum against a firm’s buy box as separate from underwriting rather than as a feature inside a pipeline tool. The workflow reads broker emails and OMs, pulls property type, pricing, and basic financials, and returns a fit score before anyone opens a spreadsheet.

Speed matters more in a market where the bid-ask spread has stayed wide and sellers are selective about counterparties. An investor able to move from teaser to credible offer in days rather than weeks is more attractive on assets where the seller has a reason to transact quickly, and some firms are winning deals on certainty of execution rather than on price.

Lending is seeing a similar compression. Credit packages have traditionally been assembled over weeks, with analysts pulling rent rolls, abstracting leases, reconciling operating statements, and building comparables by hand. A 2026 TIMVERO survey found institutions running purpose-built AI underwriting platforms reporting a 40 to 60 percent reduction in analyst time per commercial loan. That shortens the window between quote and term sheet and lets a lender reprice as conditions move during the process rather than carrying stale assumptions to closing.

Portfolio review is moving to a continuous cadence as well. Hold-sell decisions have historically run annually or semiannually because evaluating each asset against current market conditions was substantial work. Running that analysis against live data surfaces the assets that have drifted from their original thesis closer to when the drift happens.

Nearly everyone reports doing something with AI, though what they are getting from it varies widely. Dealpath’s 2026 State of AI in CRE Investing, a vendor survey of more than 100 institutional investment and technology professionals, found 97 percent of respondents with AI integrated somewhere in their investment process. Only 5 percent of firms in JLL’s survey report having achieved all their AI program goals, and Deloitte’s 2026 Commercial Real Estate Outlook found 27 percent running into real implementation problems including technical issues, lack of expertise, and internal resistance.

For the first time in fifteen years of JLL’s research, talent shortage outranked budget as the primary obstacle to creating value in corporate real estate. Teams lack people who can take AI output and convert it into an investment decision rather than a report.

Screening ten times more deals also creates an exposure that did not exist before, which is maintaining diligence depth across a much larger pipeline. The consequences of thinner underwriting show up at the investment committee rather than at the screening stage, which is late enough to be expensive.

JLL’s research found the organizations getting the most from AI share four characteristics, and none of them involve the tools themselves. Those firms are committed to growing their workforce, have built organizational resilience into how they operate, maintain a long-term strategic view, and have their HR, IT, and real estate functions working together rather than separately.

The pressure to move faster is not going to ease. Business planning horizons are unlikely to lengthen, the leases signed this year will still be in place when the next set of assumptions turns over, and the firms able to evaluate more deals in less time will keep having first conversations with sellers who want certainty. What that produces is an advantage built on organizational capability rather than on access to tools everyone can buy.

item.title: Northern California MLS Expands Brokerages’ War Over Exclusive Listing Rules
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
MLSListings joins six other multiple listing services suing Compass over alleged pressure to drop fines for pre-marketing rule violations.

The post Northern California MLS Expands Brokerages’ War Over Exclusive Listing Rules appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
MLSListings, a Northern California multiple listing service, filed an amended complaint on Oct. 30 joining six other MLSs in a lawsuit against Compass in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. The original suit, filed Oct. 21 by Arizona Regional Multiple Listing Service, BridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS, Hive MLS, and REcolorado, accuses Compass of pressuring the organizations to stop fining agents who violate pre-marketing and listing submission rules. MLSListings said it received a demand letter from Compass on Sept. 8.

MLSListings President and CEO Dave Wetzel said publicly marketed homes withheld from the shared marketplace harm buyers, sellers, and smaller brokerages. Compass countered that seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, already permit agents to publicly market office exclusives without fines. The brokerage said none of the problems the plaintiffs warn about have materialized in those markets.

Compass said it plans to file a motion to dismiss in the case. The dispute reflects growing tension over how MLSs enforce data-sharing rules that have historically formed the foundation of brokerage cooperation. Separately, three Compass-affiliated agents plan to request a judge quash subpoenas issued in the National Association of Realtors’ legal battle with ThePLS.com.

item.title: What Designers Are Finally Getting Right About Office Noise
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Noise consistently ranks among the top complaints in open workplaces, and designers are moving past white noise toward natural soundscapes and tools that let clients hear a space before construction.

The post What Designers Are Finally Getting Right About Office Noise appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
The experience-driven office has been the dominant design idea of the past several years. Owners competing for tenants and companies competing for attendance have invested in better light, better air, better food, better furniture, and better views. The logic holds that people will choose to come in if the building gives them something home cannot.

Acoustics has been the slowest of those elements to get attention despite consistently ranking as the thing people complain about most. Oxford Economics research found noise distraction to be the top complaint among open plan workers, and more than half of non-executive employees report that ambient noise reduces their satisfaction and productivity. A building can get everything else right and still leave people unable to concentrate.

Designing for sound is complicated by the fact that people want different things from it, and the same person wants different things depending on the task. Rather than designing to an average, Ben Sachwald, AKRF’s Senior Vice President and Director of Acoustics, Noise, and Vibration, argues for building range into the floor plate. “It is better to cluster your noisier spaces together and then provide a gradient as you go further away,” he said. “This gives people options. The approach that we take is to remember that no two brains are identical and different tasks and moods can call for different situations.”

How designers treat the sound within those zones has also changed. The standard tool for decades was sound masking, usually filtered white or pink noise played through ceiling speakers to raise the background level enough that nearby conversation becomes unintelligible. It reduces speech distraction effectively and most people dislike how it feels.

Natural sound has emerged as the alternative, and Sachwald sees it as part of a broader misunderstanding about what biophilic design involves. “Some people still think biophilic design just means more plants in the space,” he said. “That is an element but it is much bigger than that.”

Biophilic soundscaping is the term for the practice, and the research behind it goes back further than the current interest. A 2015 study in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America found that natural sound masking in open-plan offices outperformed silence, with cognitive functioning holding higher across the workday. More recent research conducted in a London workplace by Kinda Studios with researchers from Goldsmiths, University of London found participants scoring 12 percent higher on creative thinking under a natural soundscape than under typical office sound, completing cognitive tasks faster without losing accuracy.

Which sound belongs in which space depends on what the space is for, and the choice is more deliberate than picking something pleasant. “In some areas you do want masking so you can use something more like a babbling brook,” Sachwald said. “To bring in energy, you might want waves crashing or birds chirping or have soft, peaceful music playing.” Water sounds are steady and predictable, which is why they cover speech well in focus areas. Birdsong and wave patterns vary enough to pull attention, which makes them better suited to a lobby than a quiet floor.

Architectural renderings have given clients a way to see a space before it exists, and sound has had no equivalent. AKRF built one, a facility in Midtown Manhattan called PinDrop that functions as a floating room within a room, acoustically isolated with an extremely low baseline sound level and a neutral response. The room runs a 10.1 channel Genelec playback system and carries five different acoustical treatments across its walls and ceiling. A client sits in it and hears an auralization, a calibrated rendering of what their conference room will sound like, what the open floor will sound like at capacity, what a particular ceiling treatment changes about either. The project has been covered by the New York Times, the Associated Press, and Fast Company, and won an ACEC New York Engineering Excellence Gold Award.

Being able to demonstrate acoustic outcomes has pulled sound earlier into the design conversation and kept it there through construction, which is where many acoustic decisions quietly get reversed. Value engineering substitutions happen late, often without anyone evaluating the acoustic consequence. Sachwald says being able to let clients hear the difference changes those conversations. “Maybe the contractors are proposing a different product, now we can get the clients to come in and hear how that would change the acoustics,” he said.

That shift is already changing how office designers works with clients, bringing acoustic questions into early planning rather than leaving them to be solved after someone complains. Sachwald expects more of the design process to run through the room as owners get used to evaluating sound the way they evaluate everything else about a space.

The post What Designers Are Finally Getting Right About Office Noise appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Affordable Housing Transfers Face Long, Costly Repairs Before Tenants See Relief
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
A Bronx building transferred to affordable housing ownership still holds 700 violations 18 months later, showing the long road from foreclosure to repair.

The post Affordable Housing Transfers Face Long, Costly Repairs Before Tenants See Relief appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
New York foreclosed on 2201-05 Davidson Avenue in the Bronx in 2025, wiping out $27 million in back taxes and transferring the 47-unit building to nonprofit Neighborhood Restore. The property will eventually move to affordable developer Lemle & Wolff, which also manages it. Tenants hoped for immediate relief, but 18 months later the building still carries more than 700 housing-code violations — more than 15 per unit. Emergency repairs have stopped leaks and restored the elevator, but floors remain unlevel and scaffolding covers the exterior.

Lemle & Wolff plans a gut rehabilitation down to the floor joists, requiring tenants to move in stages while preserving their current rents. The developer is still securing a private construction loan to supplement city financing. Rent collections have fallen since the transfer; some tenants who stopped paying under the previous owner have not resumed. Organizers from Our Bronx are pushing residents to pay rent, especially those interested in forming a housing cooperative. Affordable housing operators citywide report collections down several percentage points since the pandemic, while insurance and utility costs have climbed sharply.

City Council member Pierina Ana Sanchez is leading an effort to revive the Third Party Transfer program, which foreclosed on more than 500 properties and 7,000 units between 2008 and 2019. The program was shut down after a class action lawsuit alleged the city took buildings without paying just compensation; the city proposed a $60 million settlement this fall. Sanchez’s SAFER Homes Act would add safeguards for owners before foreclosure. Another Bronx building transferred through the program, 1968 Marmion Avenue, took eight years to complete its renovation, offering a timeline for what Davidson tenants may face.

New York Wants to Turn Distressed Buildings Into Affordable Housing. What Happens While They’re Waiting?

item.title: Houston Developer Hines Joins Race for European Individual Investor Capital
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Hines launches European Long-Term Investment Fund targeting wealthy individuals across Europe, Asia Pacific, and Latin America with open-ended real estate vehicle.

The post Houston Developer Hines Joins Race for European Individual Investor Capital appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Hines received regulatory approval to launch the Hines Global Real Estate Opportunities strategy, an open-ended evergreen vehicle structured as a European Long-Term Investment Fund. The fund will initially target individual investors in Europe, with plans to expand distribution to Asia Pacific, Latin America and Canada. Hines already operates the Hines Global Income Trust in the US, which held $7.3 billion in gross asset value as of September. The Houston-based firm manages $91 billion in assets globally.

The Eltif structure allows periodic redemptions and requires no minimum investment, though managers typically ask for at least €10,000. More than 250 private market funds launched under the Eltif framework since 2024, following regulatory reforms that made the vehicles more accessible to retail investors. Infrastructure currently dominates Eltif assets, while real estate accounts for just 6.6% of the total €18.2 billion in open-end Eltif holdings as of September. The Hines fund will maintain an externally managed liquidity reserve to meet quarterly redemption requests.

Hines joins Blackstone, Apollo and other alternative asset managers expanding their retail distribution channels in Europe. The firm hired Paul Ferraro from Carlyle in 2024 to lead its global private-wealth solutions strategy, then brought on former Schroders executive Eugenio Cicconetti to build out its European wealth division. Fund launches continued at a similar pace in 2026 despite concerns about private capital managers’ exposure to software companies and loan quality, with some firms shifting focus to infrastructure or multi-strategy vehicles.

US Property Titan Hines Targets Europe’s Rich With New Fund

item.title: The Opposition of New Power Lines Could Spread Beyond Data Centers
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Aging grids need massive infrastructure upgrades

The post The Opposition of New Power Lines Could Spread Beyond Data Centers appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
5 days 23 hr agoNov. 2, 2026 2:47 pm

Spending on the transmission system by investor-owned utilities and transmission companies is expected to reach $43.7 billion this year, up about 10 percent from last year’s estimate, according to the Edison Electric Institute. Much of the country’s power infrastructure dates to the decades after World War II and is due for replacement regardless of what the AI buildout does, but the growth in demand has turned a maintenance cycle into a generational expansion. The fights over where those lines go are now showing up in places that have nothing to do with data centers.

Virginia’s Loudoun County tracked 233 data center buildings completed or under construction as of March, and the grid serving them has to be rebuilt to match. Dominion Energy’s annual electricity demand growth across Virginia and North Carolina has jumped to roughly 5.5 percent from the 1 to 2 percent range it sat in before 2022. Greg Mathe, Dominion’s director of electric transmission engagement, permitting and land, attributes most of that to data centers while noting that electrification and manufacturing growth, including pharmaceuticals, are contributing as well.

In Ashburn, a 500-kilovolt line the utility classifies as a backbone reliability project is routed through a residential backyard that abuts a wooded conservation easement, requiring a 165-foot monopole and the removal of hundreds of trees. The homeowners association donated land at the rear of the neighborhood to the local school system in an attempt to block the path, since Virginia utilities generally lack standard eminent domain authority over county governments and school boards. The state utility commission approved the route anyway, and the dispute is headed to the Virginia Supreme Court on appeal.

Similar disputes are running in Texas, where high-voltage lines proposed to crisscross the state would bisect ranch land northwest of Austin, and in Georgia, where Southern’s Georgia Power plans to tear down 29 homes along a 35-mile line. Clay Rikard, senior vice president of system planning at Southern, points to a voluntary agreement rate above 99 percent and says condemnation is rare, framing the work as broadly beneficial. “Data centers do represent a lot of the growth, but I think they’re also bringing tremendous benefits to our communities,” he said, adding that new transmission also allows older plants to retire and makes it possible to move power in from other regions.

Utilities have an institutional reason not to tie a given line to a given customer. Alexandra Klass, an energy law professor at the University of Michigan Law School, notes that transmission projects are usually justified on congestion grounds rather than by naming a project, since the congestion is real and the need is broad. That framing is accurate and also politically necessary, and it is exactly what makes the current moment difficult. A line justified by general reliability still lands in a specific backyard, and the homeowner has no particular reason to believe the general justification.

The part that should concern anyone building anything large is that opposition organized around data centers does not stay organized around data centers. Transmission capacity is shared infrastructure. The same 500-kilovolt line that serves a hyperscale campus also serves the industrial park, the hospital expansion, the manufacturing plant, and the thousand-unit residential project that needs an interconnection five years out. Communities that successfully delay or reroute a line are not constraining one development. They are constraining everything downstream of it.

Eminent domain reform is becoming part of the conversation. Property owners who settled with utilities have started arguing publicly that the legal process favors institutions with counsel over individuals without it, and state legislatures are listening in several of the markets where transmission buildout is heaviest. Any procedural changes that result will apply to pipelines, roads, and water infrastructure as readily as to power lines. This might help move projects along in the short term but could result in even more politcal backlash that could

We would expect the political energy currently aimed at data centers to outlast the particular projects that generated it, because the underlying objection is to high-voltage infrastructure crossing residential land rather than to what sits at the end of the wire. Developers in markets with constrained interconnection queues may find that the capacity they are counting on has become harder to build for reasons that have nothing to do with their own project.
